subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to bring flax and rye under the jurisdiction of the Canadian wheat board so as to end speculation with respect to these grains on the Winnipeg grain exchange. Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce arising out of a series of messages received during the last few days from various marketing points in western Canada to the effect that there is again a very pronounced shortage of cars needed

Inquiries of the Ministry to move wheat. Would the minister say what has been done recently to remove any discrimination as between marketing points and to assure reasonable equality of opportunity to all marketing points to dispose of their wheat?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hardly
believe there can be a shortage of box cars. However, there is a limitation on shipments to the lakehead, as is usual at this season of the year, for the reason that the storage space at the lakehead is filled to capacity and cars can be unloaded only as all-rail shipments from lakehead elevators are made to the east. However, the port of Vancouver is working to capacity and its elevator capacity is only about half filled. The difficulty there has been to get the grain forwarded rapidly enough to load the boats that have been offering. I think the railroads have done exceptionally well, although there was a serious interruption early this week when a snow slide cut off movement of grain on both railroads to the Pacific coast.
The wheat board is charged with the responsibility for these movements, and I have received no reports that there has been any deterioration in the situation. However, in view of the question asked by the Leader of the Opposition I will make inquiries of the wheat board to make sure that the operation is proceeding normally for this time of year.

Can the
minister say whether special consideration is being given to the supplying of box cars to points with a one or two-bushel quota, or if he would consider this question as well in his discussions with the board?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
To clear up that situation, first of all, I can say that there are at this time no points on a one-bushel quota in western Canada. There are a number of points on a two-bushel quota

not too many. But the situation as compared with that of a year ago is some 65 million or 70 million bushels better as far as the forwarding of grain from country points is concerned.
Every effort is being made to bring delivery opportunities up to a position of equality, and I think considerable progress is being made in that direction. When the one-bushel quota points were eliminated, the five-bushel quota was opened. There are now a considerable number of points on the five-bushel quota. The intention of the board has been to give preference to points that did not deliver an eight-bushel quota last year. I understand that a real effort is


being made in that direction, but I am not able to tell the house how successful it has been.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
Did I
understand the minister to say that special consideration was being given to those points, in their delivery quotas, which had been unable to deliver the crop last year or the year before?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker, priority has been given to those points. That was my instruction to the wheat board, and I know that the wheat board has been attempting to carry out that instruction. It is not as easy as it sounds, owing to the quality of the grain offered at certain points, but in general, points which did not ship their full quota last year have been receiving preference this year in the supply of box cars.

subtopic: SOCKEYE SALMON

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Tuesday, February 26, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Sinclair-Mr. Robinson (Simcoe East) in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to implement a convention between Canada and the United States of America for the protection, preservation and extension of the sockeye salmon fisheries in the Fraser river system, signed at Washington on the 26th day of May, 1930, and a protocol thereto signed at Ottawa on the 28th day °f December, 1956, and for carrying out Canada's obligations under the said convention and protocol.

subtopic: SOCKEYE SALMON
subsubtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, last evening at the conclusion of my remarks I was drawing to the attention of the committee some of the problems with respect to conservation that confront the fishermen on the Fraser river itself. However, before continuing

from where I left off at that time, I wish to review some of the discussion that took place yesterday with respect to what the minister had to say as reported at page 1688 of Hansard with regard to this motion. The minister said:
We are anxious to have this bill approved as soon as possible in order that the salmon commission can begin to exercise control over these fisheries during the coming season. I might add that President Eisenhower has asked his congress to give speedy approval to the bill which he has submitted to congress.
Mr. Chairman, we in this group are extremely anxious to have this resolution carried as quickly as possible and to have the bill brought before the house for its considered attention as well. However, there are certain factors which require some clarification and it is my intention to deal with some of those very shortly.
As I mentioned yesterday, the salmon fishing industry in the province of British Columbia is a vital one to the province, and more particularly to my own area. The potential which the Fraser river as such offers to the people of British Columbia is not to be underestimated. It might well be compared with the Nile river and what it means to Egypt, in fact. Certainly the Fraser river means just as much to my own province and the people within it.
Yesterday the hon. member for Comox-Alberni drew what he considered to be a bit of unfinished business to the attention of the minister. I would certainly concur with his remarks to the effect that the original protocol and the subject matter thereof should be included with this bill as well as the present protocol that we have under consideration.
As reported at page 1688 of Hansard the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich, in speaking of Canadians out-fishing Americans, had this to say:
In order to get ahead of the United States fishermen in Puget sound our fishermen had to go farther and farther out to sea. The result of this move was a need for bigger and more expensive equipment, bigger and more expensive gear and longer hauls. It was an uneconomic process, because not only did larger fishing vessels have to be provided, but floating camps had to be sent out to service that fishing fleet.
In drawing this matter to the attention of the minister the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich failed, I think, to bring out certain other factors which possibly are not so obvious to him as they would be to the fishermen on the Fraser river but which are of great import to the people in my riding whom it is my privilege to represent.
The fact is, Mr. Chairman, we are given to understand that the fishing fleet that goes out to sea catches fish that are smaller than those

that can be caught along the seacoast. I would ask the minister, in his consideration of this question, to rectify the thinking of some of these fishermen of the Fraser valley, or prove to their satisfaction that such is not the case. They question, and I think rightly so, whether the fish which are caught at sea are of better quality than the ones which are caught, let us say, near the coast line. They also question whether there is not a greater loss by spoilage of the fish which are caught far at sea and brought to the canneries by refrigeration ships. We are given to understand now-it may be a rumour; I am not sure whether it is or not; the minister may be in a position to answer it-that quite a number of the fish which are caught at sea, in fact more than among those which are caught along the seashore, are spoiled in transit and that whole shiploads have to be dumped back into the sea. It is debatable, too, whether, so far as the industry is concerned, the quality of these fish is better for human consumption purposes. Then, a question that comes to my mind is the tonnage of the fish that is caught. If the statement is true, which the gill net fishermen tell me, that the fish at sea are smaller, and you catch more of them, are you going to have more food value so far as tonnage is concerned than you would have if you caught a bigger fish near the seacoast, but caught fewer of them?
I consider that preservation of fish is complementary to their consumption. Let me use relative figures. If the fish which are caught, let us say at sea-I know this could be wrong but I will use it as an example- numbered 2 million, and if they weighed five pounds each, what is the difference if we caught 10-pound fish along the coast and took a million of them?

I have ascertained that the entire pack of Johnston Fishing and Packing Company is again all "A" grade quality with no "B" grade fish.

We have watched the results of this closure for two years now, but have so far failed to see any improvement in the spawning of fall fish after September 15 which could be a result of the closure.

Therefore you will see that the minister's claim that it is necessary to close the area for conservation does not seem to hold water as an escapement of 2,600 out of 4,612 that entered the river is much better than most spawning returns.
Possibly the minister would like to comment on that, as he undoubtedly will, and

explain to me and to the individuals in so doing just how the change of conservation plans has increased the number of fish that have gone up the Fraser river to spawn and actually increased the stocks, because that is the purpose behind conservation measures as such.

He owes it to the house and he owes it to the fishermen themselves to give a complete report.
There is one other question which arises in connection with artificial spawning grounds and fish farming and it relates in an indirect way to a problem that is probably more properly dealt with at another time. I do not intend to debate it at this time but a question will arise concerning damming the Fraser river. Concerning the question of artificial spawning grounds I have in my hand a copy of a letter which was addressed to the Hon. James Sinclair, Minister of Fisheries. The letter is dated February 23 and comes from Innisfail, Alberta. The hon. member for Red Deer was kind enough to give me a copy of this letter which is signed by a Mr. N. Kvisle.

Possibly the minister will not mind if I put a portion of this letter on the record at this time. I hope he will find time to comment on the facts as he understands them in relation to the suggestion contained in this letter. One portion of the letter reads as follows:
Now the fact is that the Fraser system does not provide ideal spawning conditions for salmon. As a matter of fact nature in the raw seldom provides the best habitat for wildlife. We must give our conservation scientists increased opportunity to improve such habitat. Why should a sockeye salmon have to fight his way up the Fraser canyon, and up the rapids of the Thompson to reach favourable gravel beds in the Adams river when artificial spawning beds could be constructed

and maintained much nearer to the sea? At present there is much evidence to indicate that there is food available in the ocean off the coast of British Columbia for much greater numbers of salmon than at present can be hatched in available spawning beds. May I suggest that we can harvest five times as many salmon annually as we do today and still utilize fully the available hydroelectric power if we construct spawning beds according to the following plan:
From the high dams on the Fraser and Thompson a small per cent of the total flow of water could be diverted laterally into adjacent side valleys where perhaps small creeks now flow, to reach the main river further down. In such artificial side streams gravel beds and resting pools could be provided, and the precise flow desired by spawning salmon maintained with insignificant loss of flow in the main power plants. Initial steep gradient would assist in oxygenating the water, while gentle gradient nearer the main stream would facilitate the construction of pools and gravel beds. I grant that the initial cost of constructing aqueducts of diversion would be high, but we must remember that the economic benefits derived would be vastly higher.
I do not have record of it' but it occurs to me that I did read of a program along somewhat similar lines which has already been instituted in my province. The minister indicated that he intends to comment extensively when he introduces the bill and possibly he will make some comments concerning this suggestion. The letter goes on to say:
You are no doubt familiar with the procedure used to establish spawning populations of salmon in such side streams and thus divert future generations from the main stream:	Mature salmon are
stripped of roe and milt below the high dams. The eggs are fertilized and placed in the side stream. Four years later the salmon thus hatched return to the side stream to spawn.
An advantage to fishing in general of high dams is that erosion and therefore silting are eliminated, thus making it possible for the salmon to travel through clean water in its ascent from the ocean, and make the lakes created by the dams suitable habitat for trout and kokanee.
I am sure that the Minister of Public Works will be very happy about preventing erosion and it will certainly make the people of New Westminster happy if they are no longer subject to erosion down stream.
The author of this letter is a naturalist in his own right and, although the proposal he offers may have been considered by fishing experts and possibly has been instituted in certain places, I think the minister owes it to the house to explain at some point during this debate exactly what stand if any has been taken concerning this particular subject.

I would like the minister to tell the committee whether there were any discussions with the representatives of the United States in the course of negotiating this protocol concerning the question of power developments on the Fraser river. It seems to me that the greatest threat to the salmon industry on the Fraser river is not by reason of what has been going on but will be what might take place if there are dams constructed on that river. I am sure the minister will agree with me that in the long run it is far more important to decide what is to be done about the construction of dams on the river.
The Fraser river, of course, is a Canadian river. It rises up in the Yellowhead pass and empties into the sea at Vancouver just below New Westminster and one would really think that only Canadians would be involved and that we would have to decide ourselves just what was to be done in connection with that river. However, as the minister has explained on many occasions, a large portion of the salmon when they go back up the river to spawn return through United States waters and in order that there might be a fair distribution of the catch this original convention was entered into in 1930. Therefore the United States is very directly concerned with the Fraser river in that way and from the point of view of the division of the fish it could almost be called an international river.
As far as the people of British Columbia are concerned, well over half of them live in the area which is drained by the Fraser river and are vitally interested in what is done on that river. Actually over half the people of the province live in the lower mainland, from where the Fraser river runs into the plain to the coast. When you add to the number of people in the lower mainland those living further up the Fraser and those
Fisheries
living on Vancouver island who are concerned too because the fish pass the island, you have a large percentage of the total population of British Columbia who are very directly interested in these Fraser river problems; not only because of the commercial fisheries but also because of the sport fisheries.
I suggest to the minister that when he replies today he deal at some length with the question of sports fishing. As the population increases in the larger centres it becomes more and more important that these sport fisheries be retained and built up. Sometimes people are apt to forget that it is not only the commercial fisheries that are at stake in the development of this river but also the sport fishery. In Vancouver I find that more and more people are beginning to ask questions about what is to happen to the Fraser river. They do this because of their interest in sport fishing.
The minister will have seen the interim report of investigations into measures for flood control in the Fraser river basin which was published last year. Among those who signed the report were T. M. Patterson, director of the water resources branch, Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, and A. J. Whitmore, chief supervisor of fisheries, Pacific area, Department of Fisheries. The other two signatories were representatives of the provincial government. That report contains some quite startling statements about what might happen to the Fraser river fisheries. For example, we find this warning on page 54:
The Fraser river is the world's greatest spawning river lor salmon. Present knowledge indicates that salmon and steelhead trout are unable to pass a number of low dams or even one high dam without losses occurring as a result of delay. In addition the mortality to young salmon migrating to the sea over a series of low dams or an individual high dam would probably be very heavy. Any system of reservoirs such as would be required to provide an adequate degree of flood control and afford reasonable protection to the lower Fraser valley would introduce a large number of obstructions which would have a serious effect on the successful reproduction of the Fraser river salmon and steelhead trout. This reduction in the number of salmon would impose a very serious loss upon the British Columbia fishing industry.
The reference there to the system of reservoirs might also include the building of power plants. Apparently there is as yet no way in which the fishing industry can be saved if dams are put in on the Fraser river as proposed. This will mean that the people of our province and of the whole of Canada will have to face the necessity of making a decision as to whether they are willing to see the salmon industry on the Fraser river system ruined in order to have power dams installed. I believe that question is so serious

Fisheries
that it cannot be aired too much. Now is the time to have the public thoroughly informed of the pros and cons so that they can make an intelligent decision as to which policy they will favour.
I must admit that personally it seems to me unwise to wipe out an industry which is one of the most important in British Columbia, which provides a living for thousands and thousands of our people. Perhaps when the minister replies he can give us the number involved. This industry has been operated in a most efficient manner and to have it destroyed would be one of the most far-reaching and I think sad developments in the whole history of Canada. It just seems impossible to me that a course would be adopted deliberately which would bring about that result. In addition to the men who make their living in the fishing industry, and their dependents, there are the thousands and thousands who are interested in sport fishing. It would be most serious if they were to be deprived of an opportunity to indulge in that fishing.
As the minister knows, heavy pressures are being brought to bear from the other side. There has been a lot of discussion about the development of power on other rivers in British Columbia, notably the Columbia river system. Certainly this situation calls for an early start on the development of power on the Columbia river in Canada. I do not think anyone can quarrel with the suggestion made by different bodies in British Columbia, and in fact by the Minister of Fisheries himself, that the Columbia river must be developed first for power purposes because the salmon industry on that river has been destroyed already by power dams erected by the United States below the boundary. There cannot be very much difference of opinion in this house on that particular feature, that the Columbia river should be developed first, before the Fraser river fishing industry is placed in jeopardy.
I hope the minister will go further today and tell us the view of his department. This whole question may end up in an argument between the Minister of Fisheries and the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, or in an argument between the dominion government and the provincial government, or it may end up iri a violent argument between the fishing industry and the power industry. Certainly it has to be faced and I do not think we can begin too soon to focus public opinion on' the whole question.
May I repeat that from my own personal point of view I would have to be shown very
[Mr. Green.l
clearly that it was in the interests of the people of British Columbia as a whole before I would agree to any plan which would wipe out an industry such as the salmon industry on the Fraser river system.

We have heard about the gill netters on the Fraser river and their problems in getting outside coastal waters to catch fish, and I suppose I have made as many representations to the minister with regard to that as anyone in this house. But what I want to say today, Mr. Chairman, is that although the minister in his introductory remarks gave the credit for this great step forward to the Pacific salmon fisheries commission, I doubt whether at any time in the history of this house any minister has introduced as many forward looking proposals over a number of years as has the present Minister of Fisheries; and I think that what he has been able to do for the fishermen of British Columbia and elsewhere is also a reflection of the position of Canada in international affairs, because I doubt whether 20 or 25 years ago Canada would have received the consideration which the Minister of Fisheries has been able to obtain in relation to this protocol.
I think the fishermen of British Columbia will approve what is being done. It means that there will be more money going into my riding; that retail merchants will receive increased income, and that there will be greater prosperity in the greatest fishing community in Canada. I rise, now, only in order to reflect my thinking with regard to what the Minister of Fisheries has done. He is a young minister who is representing Canada in a most effective way, not only in this case but in many others, and one who has proved a true friend to the fishermen and a true friend to the fishing industry, these being two different things. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I said at the beginning of this debate on the resolution that I would make my remarks quite brief because I felt I could give a better explanation when the bill, together with its schedule, was in the hands of hon. members.
I must, first of all, thank hon. members of the opposition and hon. members on our own side who have spoken in approval of the work which has been done by the officials of my department and the international salmon commission in conserving and expanding the salmon fisheries of the west coast. They have done an excellent job, and I am very glad to be associated with that work. I will touch upon only one or two of the points which have been raised today, because the purpose of this resolution is to decide in principle whether it is advisable to introduce a measure to include pink salmon under the control of the international Pacific salmon commission.
Every hon. member who has spoken thinks it is a good thing to do. When the bill is before the house for second reading I will answer at length most of the questions which have been raised today, but there are one or two which I think should be answered now in order that the replies will be contained in the same copy of Hansard as the question.
The hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich, who has always taken a great interest in the fisheries of British Columbia, suggested, in approving of this measure, that we should also consider exercising similar control over the other three species of Pacific salmon-cohoe, spring and chum. We, of course, in our own Department of Fisheries, do exercise very close control over those fish which are entirely Canadian. An unusual feature of the sockeye and pink salmon runs heading for the Fraser river is that they come from the high seas through the outside Canadian waters, then through American waters in Puget sound, where they could be completely intercepted by American fishermen, then back into Canadian waters outside the estuary of the Fraser. Afterwards, of course, they pass up this allCanadian river.
It is because of this international aspect of the question that the negotiations in this international commission have concerned sock-eye salmon and pink salmon. This agreement provides for an equal sharing of the catch, and, as the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich pointed out, we do not admit for one moment that we should share any fish which come from the high seas, enter Canadian waters and pass then into Canadian streams.
As far as the Fraser runs of sockeye and pink salmon are concerned, they do follow the international route I have indicated, but a very substantial portion of the chums heading for the Fraser river follow an all-Canadian 82715-108
Fisheries
route. Naturally, it is not considered advantageous for Canada to include these fish under a sharing agreement.
As the hon. member pointed out, there has been a rather alarming decline in the returns of chum salmon to our British Columbia fisheries in the last two years. I say "alarming" because there are fluctuations in many fisheries. This is alarming because we had good spawning; our scientists watched the escape into the sea of the small fry, and there was good spawning. We have tightened up our conservation regulations because of the extra efficiency of our modern fishing fleet and gear, but we think that the major part of the mortality must have occurred during the three years which the salmon spent in the sea. That theory is corroborated by the fact that a similar decline has been noticed on the Siberian side by Russian and Japanese fisheries. It is one of those things about which our scientists still do not possess a great deal of information. Their knowledge of the behaviour of the fish during the time they spend in inland waters and in the rivers is improving all the time, but it is only in the last two or three years that they have acquired much knowledge of what happens to the fish out in the middle of the Pacific ocean.
The hon. member for Comox-Alberni commented on the peculiarity of the pink salmon run, pointing out that we have enormous runs during the odd-number years and very small runs-in the Fraser-in the even years. I was again interested to find out that in the great Siberian fisheries they experienced exactly the same fluctuations in these runs. Pink salmon are only two-year old salmon, so it seems difficult to explain why a stream which has produced 30 million fish in an odd year should, with the same food resources and the same beds for spawning, produce only one million in the following year.
Our scientists, in addition to Japanese, Russian and American scientists, have all been working on this problem, trying to build up the off year run. We have sought to do so by transferring fish from those streams-we have very few-in which there is a good run in the off year. The Queen Charlotte islands are one source, because there we have rivers which support a good run in the even years as well as in the odd years. The Jones creek experiment, which was commended by the hon. member was constructed by our department and the British Columbia electricity company, creating an artificial spawning bed in an effort to build up even-year pink runs.
The hon. member for Comox-Alberni also mentioned the protocol. The protocol will be attached as a schedule to the bill when it is brought forward for first reading.

Fisheries
The hon. member for New Westminster mentioned the Gordon commission report on fisheries. This was, I think, an encouraging report, because it pointed out the fact that food is becoming more and more important in the world because of the ever-increasing world population which is growing, now, at the rate of about 50 million people a year. Fifty million more mouths to feed.
Most of the suitable agricultural land in the world is already very heavily under cultivation which is why more and more the nations of the world are turning to the sea to find the extra food their people want. That is why we Canadians are especially fortunate because we are at the front door of the two greatest fisheries in the world, the north Atlantic and the north Pacific, and over the years we Canadians have done a pretty good job of conserving our own fisheries because both the total catch and total value are steadily increasing. That is in contrast to the experience of many other nations which have depleted their fisheries and now must send their fleets thousands of miles to secure the fish their people need.
The Gordon commission forecast that there would be increased production but a decreasing number of fishermen. That is all to the good too. Unfortunately, in some parts of Canada there have been marginal fishermen who fished only because there was no other occupation for them. On both coasts we have highly skilled full-time professional fishermen who can fish in any sort of weather and it is these men who will continue at the fishing. As other opportunities for employment develop in Canada we will find that these marginal fishermen will move into shore occupations, so we see a smaller number of much better fishermen sharing a bigger catch which, of course, means a higher standard of living for them.
That was particularly marked in the last season in British Columbia. Our salmon fishery out there has a four year cycle, one very big year, a second high year, a medium year and one low year. All these years are improving, but we still have a low year, which was last year. Because of that knowledge in advance over a thousand fishermen left the fishing industry for employment ashore. The catch was a small one but the price was extremely good, the best price ever paid for salmon on the west coast, and the smaller number of fishermen enjoyed larger catches and higher prices and had a very good year.
The hon. member for New Westminster wanted me to discuss in detail the growth of fish caught off the shores of the ridings of the members for Esquimalt-Saanich and

Comox-Alberni and off the estuary of the Fraser river. The average pink salmon is about 5 pounds. It may take 10 to 12 days to move from the west coast into the Fraser. I do not think there is much of an improvement in size in that time. The sockeye salmon moves even quicker. It is after all a 4 year mature fish when it comes back, and I think there will be a barely appreciable increase in growth.	.
Both the sockeye and pink salmon pretty well give up feeding when they come even close to fresh water. It is very rarely, for example, that either a sockeye or a pink salmon is caught by a lure in the territorial waters off British Columbia.

Our tagging has not shown that at all. There may be some mingling of sockeye in the centre of the Pacific ocean some 2,000 miles out to sea but the little pink salmon are so small there is not much possibility of their being out in the centre.
The Jones creek spawning experiment, which was also mentioned, is going very well. The hon. member said I had not answered the gill net fishermen about closure above the Pattullo bridge for the late runs, which was brought in two or three years ago on the advice of my scientists and officers. If there is one thing I have explained at great length to the annual convention of the fishermen's union, the officers of the fisheries association and in the House of Commons it has been that closure, and when the international salmon commission takes over the management of the pinks I am quite sure they will certainly maintain that closure on the late runs.
I was very interested to receive the letter from the man in Alberta, from which the hon. member read excerpts. It does show the very great interest there is in our fisheries when a chap from Alberta will write me a long letter giving his views on how we should preserve the salmon run against the threat of power dams. Unfortunately there are quite a number of people in this country who feel that the Department of Fisheries has done nothing about the matter, that this is some new problem suddenly emerged. Our department has been working on the problem of the movement of salmon around dams on

both coasts for at least 30 years. Our colleagues on the American side have been working on it for an equal number of years. In Scotland, Norway, Japan and Russia their scientists have been working on it, but all to no avail. It has not been through any lack of work by the most highly qualified scientists and engineers that a solution has not yet been found.
The gentleman who wrote the letter has the idea that all we have to do is to build artificial spawning beds below the last dam and our problem is solved. In his speech the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich pointed out that the valuable fishery in the Fraser is the sockeye salmon fishery, and the sockeye salmon after having hatched in the spring in the gravel beds of these little creeks, drift down and spend one year or sometimes two in a lake.
Take the Adams river run. A short 7 mile stretch of this river in the Kamloops riding produces in its peak year 12 million sockeye salmon for the commercial fishery, each worth about $2 apiece. These 12 million adult salmon came from probably 200 million salmon fry which spend a year down in Shuswap lake living off the plankton food in that lake. If we are going to hatch sockeye salmon just to replace the Adams river run alone by building a hatchery below the last power dam, construction of which is being contemplated near Hope, we would have to build as well a lake the size of Shuswap lake and see that it is filled with the necessary food.
That is why the problem of the sockeye salmon is such a difficult one. It is quite true that the moment the little pink salmon is bom it heads for the sea, uses the river only as a means of transport to get to the sea and then lives on the very abundant food resources in the sea. In the case of the pink salmon we can build, and are building, spawning beds. But that is no solution for the very difficult problem of the sockeye salmon.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, who has also shown great interest in the fishing industry, asked whether when we were discussing this new treaty with the Americans the matter of fish and power had been discussed because, of course, no matter how good a job we do in international cooperation and conservation of the sockeye and pink salmon of the Fraser river system that will all be ended if a series of ten low level dams up to 100 feet high are built on the lower Fraser and on the Thompson and an enormous 750 foot high dam is built on the upper Fraser at Moran. We did not discuss it because the Americans appreciated that this was entirely a Canadian problem 82715-1084
Fisheries
since this is a Canadian river, and power developments are in the hands of the provincial government and control of the fisheries is in the hands of the federal government. I am sure, however, that our American colleagues in the fisheries field, with whom we have worked very closely, are aware of the fact that the fisheries department is doing everything it can to ensure that we are going to continue to have this great and valuable fishery resource.
I was asked by the hon. member for Nanaimo if, when I spoke on second reading, I would give the house some details of what our officers have done in trying to solve the very difficult problem of fish and power on the Fraser and on other salmon streams. I would be very happy to do that then in detail but, because the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra has also raised the matter, I think I should summarize the problem briefly and the attitude our department takes and, for that matter, the fishing industry of British Columbia.
We have a salmon industry out there worth an average of around $50 million a year. It gives employment to 12,000 fishermen, 6,000 shore workers and a very considerable number of workers in auxiliary industries. The salmon industry of British Columbia, for example, has been worth more to the province than all the gold mined since the days of the earliest gold rush. As a food resource it is a resource which is becoming more and more important in the world.
The salmon commission has shown that it is able to expand these resources. In some ways in fishing we are far behind farming. I suppose that originally the farmer was a hunter who trapped wild animals and only later found it easier to raise wild animals and breed them more successfully. Up to now our fishing has largely been in the trapping stage. The salmon commission has taken us quite a bit further in improving on nature in by-passing falls with fish-ways; for example; in opening up areas for spawning which have been inaccessible for salmon; the general control and management of river systems to increase production and we have seen the production steadily rise. Dams in a salmon river system are a hazard in many ways. When I speak on second reading I will deal with the problem in more detail. The best scientists in the world are agreed that the proposed dams in the lower Fraser and the big single dam on the upper Fraser will completely end salmon fishing on the Fraser in just one cycle. It will not be a matter of diminishing over the years. In just one four-year cycle we will have no salmon industry. The proof is the evidence given by

Fisheries
the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra. There was a day when the Columbia river was even a greater salmon stream than the Fraser river. But the Columbia river, to all intents and purposes, is through as a salmon stream now because the Americans built the six big dams in the state of Washington and on the Washington-Oregon boundary. There are no salmon above the last dam and there are very few salmon between the first dam and the top dam. What salmon are left on the Columbia system are spawned below the lowest dam. It is pretty good evidence, as far as the people of British Columbia are concerned, of what happens to salmon streams when dams are placed on them.
The attitude of the Department of Fisheries and the fishing industry is a simple one. We know that British Columbia, because of its rapid expansion, is hungry for electrical power which, after all, is the sinews of industry. We feel that no salmon stream should be dammed until every non-salmon stream has been fully utilized. We have already carried that policy out. When the great aluminum company project was first discussed in British Columbia they wanted to go to the Chilko lake in the Cariboo, the second greatest source of salmon on the whole Fraser system. It was the fishing industry that forced them out of that project and farther inland up to Tweedsmuir park to the present Nechako-Kitimat-Kenamo site, an area in which there are no salmon. Today in British Columbia we have both the great fisheries resources from the Chilko lake system and the great power development at Kitimat.
In British Columbia today, as the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra has stated, there is one enormous source of untapped power, namely the Canadian section of the Columbia which this parliament protected by Bill No. 3 of some years ago. There are no salmon in the Canadian part of this river today because of the United States dams south of the line. If the next gig dam in British Columbia is built at Mica creek on the Columbia instead of on the Fraser, we shall have enough power for at least the next ten years if not fifteen years if that power is spread through a grid to all southern British Columbia. If however that power is to be swallowed up by a single aluminum plant at the site of the dam, then we are no further ahead as far as power needs are concerned. Instead of exporting electricity through power lines, we are going to be exporting packaged electricity in the form of ingots of aluminum. Hence we feel very strongly that the British Columbia Power Commission or the British Columbia Electric

Company or some other agency should develop the power in the Canadian section of the Columbia and before the Fraser is touched.
There is a second development in British Columbia in the power field, and that is because of the rapid growth of the oil and gas business. Today we have the West Coast Transmission Company pushing its line down to Vancouver. We have both the public utility, the British Columbia power commission and the privately owned company, the British Columbia electric company, building enormous gas turbines to produce power for Vancouver and for Vancouver island. The cost of electric energy produced from thermal sources-that is from coal or oil or gas-must be getting fairly close to the cost of new water installations in British Columbia because the hydro installations which are left are the most expensive ones. The easy, cheap, accessible ones have long since been built.
There is a third thing in which we are all interested. Canada is now the second producer of uranium in the world and very shortly is expected to be the greatest producer of uranium in the world. The British are first in the commercial use of uranium for the production of power. They now have two commercial units in operation at Calder Hall producing a total of 92,000 kilowatts at a price very slightly above the price of power produced from coal in Britain. After all, Britain was built on her coal resources. We, of course, are building our first commercial plant in conjunction with the province of Ontario and the Canadian General Electric Company up near Chalk River. Since we are just on the horizon of this atomic age it would be a tragedy if we dammed the Fraser for power and so lost our salmon industry and then in the end found that atomic energy was cheaper and more practicable than hydro power. That is again why we feel very strongly that the Mica creek development must be gone ahead with as quickly as possible because it will take the entire pressure off the Fraser river for at least ten years.
I must say that so far we have had good co-operation from both the British Columbia electric company, the British Columbia power commission and every other industry in British Columbia which uses water. Up to now we have shown that we can have fish and power and we hope to continue to be able to do that.
One group that we cannot deal with very co-operatively is a group of United States promoters with no interest in our province other than to make a fast profit out of power

development and who are using a local college professor and a local lawyer as their spokesmen. These laymen blandly assert that the problem of moving fish over dams could be very quickly solved if we just put our minds to it. I mentioned the point that it is difficult to co-operate with a group like that because they have no real interest in our province. They do not appreciate, as do all members from British Columbia, the very real value of this great salmon industry to our province. Nor do they realize that that value is going to steadily increase over the years.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra mentioned one other point which is perhaps not directly relevant to this discussion, namely the value of our sports fishery in British Columbia. We British Columbians are, of course, accustomed to comparisons made by Atlantic members with regard to the superiority of the Atlantic salmon as a sporting fish over our western salmon. I, as Minister of Fisheries, responsible for both these groups, will not make any comment on that matter.

subsubtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES
speechtext: You know where your heart lies.

speechtext:
The fact remains that we have salmon sport fisheries out on the west coast. We have probably 50,000 people who are sports fishermen on the west coast and who pursue the spring and the cohoe salmon. These sports fishermen are our greatest allies in this battle between the fish interests and the power interests. It is hard to place a dollar value on the pleasure that our Canadians get from fishing, without licences, in our seas for these salmon. We made a report a year ago. We think that probably about a quarter of a million salmon and grilse are caught by our sports fishermen each year in our waters.
As I say, this matter is not quite relevant to this resolution, which is concerned not with spring and cohoe salmon but with sockeye and pink salmon, neither of which will take a lure. But the whole salmon fishery is knit together to conserve our fisheries resources against the pressure to develop salmon streams for the production of power.
I have not covered all the points raised by hon. members when they spoke for I think we all want the bill to come forward as quickly as possible. When we are on the bill I intend to give a review of what the salmon commission has done in the last 20 years, what it has meant financially to our province to have that expansion in the fisheries. I will indicate the type of program I think they will be able to carry out in
Fisheries
conserving and restoring the pink salmon fisheries and what the cost of that program will be.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in his speech the minister made some reference to the question I raised last night about the protocol. Apparently he must have misunderstood the purport of my remarks last night, because I said I assumed that the protocol which has to do directly with inclusion of the pink salmon would be attached as a schedule to the bill; but the protocol to which I had particular reference and which I suggested should be considered also for inclusion as a schedule at this time was the protocol of the exchange of ratification of July 28, 1937.
In his reference to my speech the minister, as I understood him, referred only to the protocol with respect to pink salmon. He gave no indication as to what his reaction was to my proposal of last night in regard to doing what I called tidying up our last arrangement with respect to this protocol of the exchange of ratification. I had hoped that he might give some indication at least that when the bill comes forward provision will be made for consolidating that protocol of exchange of ratification in a way that it would intelligently be part of the general documentation of the treaty.

speechtext:
I think the hon. member will find that the amended protocol, which is in the schedule, covers both the original protocol of 1937 and the agreement signed last December between the two governments.
I might point out that as far as the parliamentary procedure which was followed in 1937 is concerned, it is not necessarily the custom of this house to ratify every international treaty. In this case we bring it before the house for ratification because we intend to take legislative action on it. The custom in recent years has become more common to bring most treaties before the house, trade treaties and other treaties, for ratification by resolution. That is probably why in 1937 the actual protocol was not ratified in the house; but if the hon. member is interested I will certainly get our copy on file in the department copied and it will be made available at least to the members when they meet in the standing committee on marine and fisheries to discuss the bill clause by clause.

subtopic: SOCKEYE SALMON
subsubtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES
speechtext:
I make just one observation regarding the run of chum salmon to which I referred. I am, of course, fully aware that the major run comes around the northern side of Vancouver island and down through the Johnstone straits. Chum salmon are caught on both sides of the strait of Juan de Fuca, on the Canadian and on the United

Fisheries
States sides. I do not know the extent, and I do not think anybody knows, of the chum run through the strait of Juan de Fuca, and I was only suggesting that during the next six years study be made of that run through those straits in order to see whether it is perhaps a larger run than we anticipate or know of at the moment. At that time, after further study, it could be considered whether a further protocol ought to be added and chum salmon considered by the commission in the future.

subtopic: SOCKEYE SALMON
subsubtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Yes. That is a very sound suggestion, because now the salmon commission will be doing these very extensive studies, tagging and catching the fish for research purposes in this whole convention area. They will incidentally catch a fair number of springs, cohoes and chums, and that is why in the protocol there is this thought that in the six-year study period the commission will also devote attention to these three types. It may well be that they should be included six years from now in a general protocol covering all the salmon fisheries of the Fraser.
On the other hand, if it turns out that at least half the chums come down the Johnstone straits to the Fraser in Canadian waters all the way, it would be difficult to include the chums for this reason. Our fishery agreements are built upon the principle of an equal division of the catch. We have openings and closings in the United States waters and in the Canadian waters from day to day to try to get the catch as equal as possible; but if in the Canadian catch are included fish that came all the way in Canadian waters, then obviously we are not going to get our full share of the fish which came through international waters.
That is why we want to be very certain of our next step. But as to the suggestion, because of the new powers that are given to the salmon commission they will be doing such a study on the other three species and will be in a pretty good position, I think, six years from now to say whether they can exercise such a control and still manage a fifty-fifty division of the catch.

subtopic: SOCKEYE SALMON
subsubtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES
speechtext:
The minister made one or two observations on which I should like to comment. First, there is the fact that he indicated to the fishermen's union and other associations that conservation had paid off with the closure of the river above Pattullo bridge during certain seasons of the year. I am not a member of the fishermen's union. If the minister has a copy of the address he may have given on that occasion I would very much appreciate it if 1 could get that information for myself so I would be familiar with
[Mr. Pearkes.l
how it had been determined that conservation has paid off better with the closure as it is instituted today as compared with three years ago before we had the change.
There is another matter to which the minister referred, and that is the question I raised earlier with respect to mid-ocean fisheries. I am not sure whether the minister misunderstood me, but the information I have comes from the submission of the united fishermen and allied workers union to the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects.
I am quite sure the minister is familiar with it. On page 7 of this submission they say:
There would be little point in fishing closures to permit escapement of salmon to the spawning grounds in British Columbia if a major part of both mature and immature fish are caught in midocean before returning to our waters.
Our fishermen are thus faced with a double handicap. First, in the interests of conserving and developing this resource we are properly restrained from excessive fishing in our own waters, but the Japanese deep-sea fishermen are under no such restraint and are in a position to cancel out the benefit of our conservation measures.
That, of course, is part of what I had specifically referred to. I realize 1 had to make interjections to make myself somewhat clearer, but that specifically was what I was referring to. At page 8 the submission goes on:
Secondly, the unrestrained fishing of the Japanese results in a curtailment of our markets and lowering of the prices received by us.
Farther on in the submission, at the same page, the united fishermen and allied workers union indicate more specifically what I possibly had in mind. The minister spoke of the fish possibly weighing slightly better than four pounds just off the coast as compared with a lesser weight on going into the river. He did not think there was too much difference in the weight of the fish at sea and in the river or in Hecate strait, let us say, or in Johnstone strait itself.
Paragraph 3 on page 8 reads as follows:
In principle, we are opposed to a mid-ocean salmon fishery which will open the salmon runs to exploitation by all nations to the detriment of those nations which maintain the spawning grounds. Also such fishing presents a major threat against any program of rehabilitation and conservation.
Paragraph 4, which is a follow-up to paragraph 3, reads:
A large proportion of salmon taken by Japanese expeditions in the mid-Pacific are immature, i.e. there is indiscriminate fishing of all age groups. Convincing proof is given by the fact that an average of 21 sockeye are needed to pack one case of salmon, 48 pounds, in the mid-ocean fishery as compared to 11 fish in the Alaska and British Columbia fishery.
In submitting my case I am fully aware that the figures I used were simple arithmetic. I used the figures 5 and 10 and here the figures 11 and 21 are used. I realize they

are not exactly the same figures in respect to the fish, but my figures serve the same purpose and can be worked out more rapidly. I feel the minister must have misconstrued my remarks, and I should like to have him elaborate further on this suggestion which the fishermen have made.

subtopic: SOCKEYE SALMON
subsubtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES
speechtext:
I would be very happy to do so. Concerning the first point, I said closure was made because of conservation and quality, and this was done on the advice of our scientists and officers there. If it had not been for that conservation our decline in the chum salmon run, for example, would have been still greater. However, that is a question you can raise to your heart's content when we have our scientists before the fisheries committee.
As far as the other question is concerned I assumed, as I am quite sure other hon. members assumed, that the hon. member for New Westminster was speaking of the outside Canadian fleet, because he mentioned the observation made by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich about how foolish it was to send a fleet off our shores with bigger boats and more expensive gear that was more likely to be damaged when if we were just to wait the fish would turn up themselves in our inside waters. The only reason we did it in this case was to get our share ahead of the Americans as long as they would not agree to share the whole catch.
I remind the hon. member of the treaty that was signed by the United States, Japan and Canada after the war for the very purpose of ending the situation which he has described. Before the war Japanese factory ships did lie off the coast of Alaska with 30 or 40 attendant catcher boats and with many miles of gill nets spread across the ocean picking up both mature and immature fish, either mature fish heading for spawning streams in Alaska or immature fish simply spending that part of their life in that part of the ocean. The fishermen of the United States suffered far more than we did, but unquestionably we suffered too because some of those fish off the Alaskan shore were moving down toward British Columbia streams, especially the Skeena and the Naas. We signed this treaty under which for 10 years the Japanese agreed to stay in their half of the ocean that is west of the 175th parallel, and we agreed to stay in our half of the ocean for any type of fish which was under scientific study which had been fully exploited, conserved and protected.
The three main fisheries of British Columbia, the salmon, herring and halibut, of course all met those specifications, so we have
Fisheries
not had any Japanese factory ships on our side of the ocean exploiting our fish. It may be that there is some slight mingling in the centre of the ocean-it is a very big ocean- between the salmon which have left the Siberian streams and the salmon which have left our British Columbian and Alaskan streams.
As far as the pink salmon is concerned it is highly unlikely, because they are only a small five-pound fish at maturity and they cannot go that far. The sockeye are out there for four years and the springs may be there for five years, so it is possible that the big ones may get that far. Some of the Siberian fish may turn up over here and some of our fish over there. We have no evidence of that, because it is only in the last three years that we have begun this high-seas tagging. The three nations had 25 ships out during the past year doing the high-seas tagging to see where these fish would turn up.
That was one of the main reasons I was so anxious to have the contact with the Russian scientists on the occasion of my visit there, because they have major salmon streams on that side and they did not belong to this international commission; yet unless they reported that our tags had turned up and unless we could report to them on their tags we would be blank in that field of knowledge. They have integrated their tagging program with ours, so we will have an answer to that problem within the next three or four years. It takes four years for the sockeye cycle and five years for the spring salmon cycle in order to get any substantial evidence.
However, I had some very striking evidence myself of the value of the north Pacific treaty to Canada and the United States during the time I lay in the little fishermen's hospital in Petropavlost on the Kamchatka peninsula. That is the centre of the major Russian salmon fishery. I had with me the deputy minister of fisheries for Russia. Every day he would fly away to take a look at the canneries and come back in the evening feeling more and more annoyed because they had the poorest catch in many years. Just over the horizon this enormous Japanese high seas fleet was lying with miles and miles of net intercepting the salmon returning to the Siberian rivers.
It was pointed out to me that the result of the action of Canada in signing this treaty had been to force the Japanese to operate entirely on the Asian side of the Pacific, working on Russian salmon. It was no great sacrifice to us to abstain from fishing in that half of the ocean because we had never

Exchequer Court Act
fished there, nor had the United States. We have now begun to accumulate sufficient tagging information so that we are going to be able to substitute a better line than just the 175th parallel. We will be able to say exactly where this line of demarcation between fish spawned in Japan or Siberia- mostly Siberia-and the fish spawned in North America stands, and how far out they go and then come back; and that line will be the boundary.
Some of the leaders of the fishermen's union have taken a curious stand in consistently opposing this treaty. It has been extremely difficult to understand that opposition if you base your thinking simply on fisheries facts; nevertheless that north Pacific treaty has been a great aid to the Canadian and United States fisheries in confining this very large and successful Japanese fleet to the other side of the ocean.
As far as high seas fishing is concerned, in the treaty we undertake to abstain from high seas fishing for salmon. We have never done it, nor have the United States. We feel it is very much more economical to wait until the salmon are mature, as was suggested by the hon. member for New Westminster, at which time they come into our own zone where they can be caught and quickly transported to the canneries.
Resolution reported and concurred in.
Mr. Sinclair thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 180, to implement a convention between Canada and the United States of America for the protection, preservation and extension of the sockeye salmon fisheries in the Fraser river system, signed at Washington on the 26th day of May, 1930, and a protocol thereto signed at Ottawa on the 28th day of December, 1956.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING PLACE OF RESIDENCE AND SALARY OF REGISTRAR
speechtext:
I am sure it requires no explanation to convince the committee that the present limitation on the residence of the registrar of the exchequer court ought to be

removed in these days of motor cars. There certainly is not, if there ever has been, any justification for the limitation imposed by the statute upon the residence of the registrar of the exchequer court.
However, the amendment introduces one other change. Hitherto the salary of the registrar has been fixed by the statute at a maximum figure of $7,500. The amendment now before the committee will have the effect of removing that limitation and allowing the salary to be determined and fixed by the governor in council. This is in keeping with a trend which has appeared in many amending bills in recent years. There have been occasions when we of the official opposition have taken issue with this trend. There have been many cases where it was felt that it was sound legislative practice to name the salary in the statute itself.
One does not wish to be dogmatic about matters of this kind, because it is not every individual in the public service in the largest sense whose salary should be rigidly fixed by statute. However, I think the committee is entitled to a word of explanation from the Minister of Justice as to why this change is being made by this bill.
hflr. Garson: Mr. Chairman, hon. members will recall that formerly a similar ceiling was placed upon the salary of the registrar of the supreme court, but that was removed last year by legislation. The hon. member for Eglinton is quite right in saying that was the fact for quite a long period of time, and it so continues in relation to certain officials of the government. For example, the Governor General of Canada, the provincial lieutenant governors, members of the cabinet, members of boards like the income tax appeal board, transport board and so on, all have their salaries fixed by statute.
It was felt that in connection with the registrar of the Supreme Court of Canada and the registrar of the exchequer court that their duties were more analogous to those of other civil servants than to those of the dignatories to whom I have just referred. On that account the simplest and most satisfactory thing to do was to remove this statutory ceiling; then their registrar's salaries could be dealt with by the governor in council in the ordinary way that salaries of civil servants are adjusted from time to time.
Clause 1 agreed to.
