speakeroldname: Hon. James Sinclair (for the Minister of Trade and Commerce) moved
subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. 46, to amend the Export Credits Insurance Act.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. H. Dickey (Parliamentary Assistant, for the Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to amend the Export Credits Insurance Act in two respects; first, to authorize the corporation to provide insurance for certain transactions which it cannot now cover-this is an amendment for which there has been considerable demand on the part of Canadian exporters -and, second, to allow the corporation to deduct for income tax purposes amounts required by the corporation for the setting up of reserves for possible losses in accordance with the requirements of its act of incorporation.
With respect to the first of these two purposes, I might say that at the present time the corporation insures exporters of goods shipped from Canada against losses occasioned by non-payment by foreign buyers due to credit and political risks involved in foreign trade. Some of the risks covered are the insolvency of a foreign buyer, cancellation of import licences in the buyer's country and the risk of delay in the transfer of funds due to foreign exchange difficulties.
Under the proposed amendment the corporation will be able to provide insurance to cover various types of export business for which there is an increasing demand in Canada, and which is available to exporters in other countries through the various types of export credit insurance organizations which are active in those countries. If this amendment is approved by the house the corporation will be authorized to provide insurance in connection with goods shipped abroad for exhibition purposes in other countries, or on consignment for sale. The corporation will also be authorized to insure sales made abroad by foreign subsidiaries of Canadian companies. Protection will be available to Canadian companies in connection with the rendering of engineering construction, technical or similar services performed in foreign countries or in connection with the supply of goods to foreign buyers, and the corporation will be authorized to provide insurance in connection with such expenses abroad 82715-109
Export Credits Insurance Act for installation, servicing, procurement of materials and labour as may be incurred by Canadian exporters of capital goods or services, expenses which form a minor but integral part of this type of business.
It might be of interest to hon. members if I were at this stage to say a word with respect to the experience of the Export Credits Insurance Corporation since it first issued a policy in September, 1945. During the 11 years of operation up to September 30, 1956, the corporation insured export sales amounting to $350 million for which it charged premiums of $3.2 million. This is an average premium of less than 1 per cent. Gross claims paid to policy holders total $7.7 million, and recoveries of $4.3 million have been obtained. Write-offs amount to only $176,000, so there are outstanding claims totalling $3.3 million in connection with which substantial recoveries are hoped for. However, since the bulk of these claims represent blocked funds held abroad, there is no means of knowing when recoveries may come in or the rate at which they may come in when some recovery is possible.
The corporation is, under its act, intended to operate on a self-sustaining basis, and at the end of September last the premiums and interest on its capital after paying net claims and operating expenses resulted in a balance held in the underwriting reserve of $1.5 million.

subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext: What date was that?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext:
I believe these figures are all as of the 30th September, 1956.
In keeping with sound insurance practice, the corporation maintains an underwriting reserve against future losses. The act of incorporation provides that the entire excess of the corporation's premium income and interest on investments over expenses and losses is to be credited to the underwriting reserve until such time as the reserve reaches the figure of $5 million. The corporation is a proprietary crown company listed in schedule D to the Financial Administration Act, and as such is subject to income tax. The Income Tax Act does not make any provision for the corporation setting up reserves for future losses, and the proposed amendment under this bill will authorize the corporation to deduct amounts credited to the underwriting reserve in calculating its income tax for the taxation year 1957 and thereafter.
As I pointed out to the house a moment ago, these credits will be made in accordance with the provision of the act until the underwriting reserve, which now stands at about $1.5 million, reaches a total of $5 million, which is the maximum provided for under the act of incorporation.

Export Credits Insurance Act

subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, often it is not easy to isolate or define the principle of a short bill to amend an existing statute, and in this particular case where we have before us a bill which offers two amendments to the act, the two being quite dissimilar and unrelated in their nature, it is more than normally difficult to define the principle of the bill. And because these two matters do involve detail, and will call for an extended discussion and the asking of many questions, no doubt, in the interests of seeking adequate information, it seems to me that consideration of the measure can best proceed in committee rather than that the debate on second reading should be extended.
May I say briefly, however, that with the purpose of the act itself we have been in sympathy so far as it helps, on fair terms, our Canadian exporters to expand their sales abroad.
The business that has been transacted by the Export Credits Insurance Corporation in the 12 years it has been in existence is substantial. The last time the measure was before the house was three years ago, at the 1954 session, when a number of amendments were made to the act, one of them relating to this underwriting reserve which is one of the subjects that arises again in the bill now under discussion.
The widening of the scope of the insurance which the corporation is permitted by the statute to write will have the effect, if the amendment is adopted, of bringing our act into line to a greater degree with the provisions of the British legislation and also the Australian legislation which, I understand, has been amended in recent times to bring the scope of the insurance that may be written under its terms into line with that which may be written under the British legislation. The credit and political risks involved in foreign trade, let us hope, are not going to be as great as they used to be, although the volume of trade in the world may be expanding.
In general, one may say that if there is to be an Export Credits Insurance Corporation engaged in the business of insuring sales by Canadian exporters against these credit and political risks, then the expansion that is proposed in this measure is a reasonable enlargement.
As to the other subject matter of amendment, I think in the committee we shall seek a good deal more information to justify the proposal to exempt from taxation that portion of the income of the Export Credits Insurance Corporation which would otherwise be taxable under that act. That there

should be an underwriting reserve no one can question. It would be impossible for the Export Credits Insurance Corporation to make any pretence of adherence to sound insurance business principles did it not attempt to create and maintain such a reserve.
The original legislation pertaining to the Export Credits Insurance Corporation did not make any explicit provision for an underwriting reserve, but the corporation had set up that reserve itself. In the amendments of 1954 legislative recognition was given to the existence of the underwriting reserve and the amendment now embodied in section 11A of the act provides that the underwriting reserve which had been created by the corporation should be continued and also that the corporation at the end of each fiscal year, if the amount standing to the credit of the underwriting reserve is less than $5 million, should credit to the reserve the excess, if any, of its revenues over its disbursements in that fiscal year or so much of the excess as is required to increase the amount of the reserve to $5 million.
The parliamentary assistant has stated that the amount standing to the credit of the underwriting reserve at September 30, 1956, was $1.5 million. That figure, sir, is lower than the figure standing to the credit of the reserve at December 31, 1955. We have not yet, of course, the annual report of the corporation for the fiscal year ended December 31, 1956, but the annual report of the corporation for the fiscal year ended December 31, 1955, shows at page 6 that the balance at the credit of the underwriting reserve at December 31, 1955, was $2,819,326. Therefore it is evident that in the first nine months of the calendar year 1956 the underwriting reserve was drawn upon by the corporation to the extent of approximately $1,319,000.
We shall be looking for some justification of the proposal to grant exemption from income tax to the credits to be placed each year out of the earnings of the corporation in the underwriting reserve. We shall require justification, sir, because we consider the principle that was recognized by the house in 1952 in providing that these proprietary crown corporations should be equated with privately owned corporations so far as income tax treatment is concerned is a sound principle and should be adhered to.
In his statement the parliamentary assistant has indicated that the effect of the present bill, if adopted, will be to relieve the corporation of income tax on that portion of its income that it places to the credit of the underwriting reserve until that reserve reaches the statutory figure of $5 million. He

has stated that that will be the result. He has given no reason to the house to justify this departure from the principle that was recognized by the house in reference to the taxation of proprietary crown corporations.
May I remind the house, Mr. Speaker, of the statement made by Mr. Abbott as minister of finance when in 1952 he introduced the present provisions of the Financial Administration Act applicable to proprietary crown corporations or operating crown corporations such as the Export Credits Insurance Corporation. At page 1253 of Hansard of April 8, 1952, we find that Mr. Abbott said:
An interesting change I am proposing under the corporation income tax is that those crown corporations of the federal government which are designated as proprietary corporations, and hitherto have been exempt from tax, will in future pay corporate income tax to the federal government in the same manner as any privately-owned corporation. "Proprietary corporations" are those so designated under the Financial Administration Act, and generally speaking are companies which are carrying on business operations similar to and in competition with private business. One desirable result of this proposed action will be to make the financial statements of these crown companies more comparable with private industry, and make it easier to assess the relative efficiency of their operations. I do not expect this change to have appreciable net revenue effects. It will increase our tax receipts and reduce our non-tax revenue.
And further:
All crown company profits eventually find their way into the treasury, and many of them already remit all or the greater part of their profits year by year.
There the minister was stating the principle that proprietary crown corporations should be subject to income tax just like any privately owned corporation. The Export Credits Insurance Corporation is one of these proprietary crown corporations. It is so designated in schedule D of the Financial Administration Act. Having regard to the fact that the principle enunciated by the then minister of finance in 1952, which I have quoted, was recognized by the government then as sound and was approved by the house, I think without objection, and certainly has been given full approval by the house from that time to this, why that principle should be departed from in this instance has not been explained by the parliamentary assistant.
I am saying now, Mr. Speaker, that when we go into committee of the whole on the bill we shall require ample justification before we are satisfied that there should be any departure from the sound principle that was enunciated and adopted in 1952. I think this matter will warrant extended discussion in the committee. As much of the discussion will depend upon the information to be supplied to the committee and will be the 82715-1094
Export Credits Insurance Act occasion of question and answer, I do not think I can add anything useful at this stage. As far as this measure proposes an extension in the scope of the insurance which the corporation is authorized to transact, it appears on the surface to be reasonable, at any rate sufficient to warrant the bill going to the committee.

subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the Export Credits Insurance Act, since it came into operation in 1945, has served a useful purpose. The parliamentary assistant outlined to us the details of its operation. He told us that the Export Credits Insurance Corporation had underwritten some $350 million of Canadian exports and that this was done for a very small sum of money, namely a premium of 1 per cent. In spite of that fact the company had collected only $3.2 million in premiums; and in spite of the very great risks attached to the export business in this day and age he told us there were no losses or no substantial losses, I take it. In the statement made a year ago, in fact, it was stated that at that time there'had been a net profit of something over $100,000.
The hon. member for Eglinton has outlined the amendments that are contained in the bill and has made some comment on them. One of the amendments provides that from here on in moneys paid into the underwriting reserves will no longer be subject to income tax. The hon. member for Eglinton seemed to take a good deal of objection to that change on the ground that in 1952 the government had enunciated a principle, namely that proprietary crown corporations should pay income tax in the same way as do similar corporations privately owned and doing business in a similar field.
I have no objection; in fact I support the principle outlined in 1952. But any reading I have done on insurance in this field leads me to the conclusion that there are no private companies underwriting comparable risks in the export field, and that this is in fact a crown corporation which is providing a service in the export field which is not provided by any privately owned company. Hence I take it this is not, in the sense of the definition of 1952, a company that is competing with private companies. It would therefore seem to me that it at any rate could follow that an exemption might be made in this case and that money paid in to the underwriting reserve might not be subject to income tax in the same way as are profits made by other companies.
While this corporation has done a useful business I believe it could be used a great deal more than it has been used in the past. This corporation, operating successfully in a limited

Export Credits Insurance Act field, is another demonstration to members of the house and to the country that crown corporations can and do play a useful part in the economic life of this country. We hear members in parties other than the C.C.F. apparently saying that crown corporations are a bad thing, that goverment mixed up in enterprise or business is a bad thing, and they seem to come to the conclusion that the government should get out of all business. But if I judge correctly the trend of all parties in this house-from the things they say, the things they support and the way they vote-they are in fact, year after year, getting the country and parliament more and more involved in publicly owned corporations. This is another example of a crown corporation-public ownership-that, according to the hon. member for Eglinton and the members on the government side of the house, has performed a useful function and at least with regard to certain of the amendments which are expanding the scope of the company 1 understand they will receive support from the two parties to which I have referred.
It seems to me that we should judge the effectiveness of this company in the light of the Canadian trade picture at the present time. I think it is well known to hon. members in the house that Canadian exports today are falling far short of Canadian imports, that we have a substantial trade deficit, and that this trade deficit is causing concern to well-informed Canadians everywhere. Because it is necessary for Canada to increase its exports I think we should give consideration to an expansion of the provisions of the act and of the work of the Export Credits Insurance Corporation in order that some of this deficit may be overcome.
In order to show how substantial is the deficit at the present time, I have in my hand figures supplied to me this afternoon from our library, which indicate that in the ten months ended in October, 1956, our exports totalled $3,967 million as compared with imports of $4,781 million; so that within the first ten months of 1956 we were running the very substantial trade deficit of some $814 million.

subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext: It was $1,290 million for the full year.

subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext:
Apparently there are later figures actually published, Mr. Speaker. I am informed that the total for the full year is some $1,290 million. In the light of that very substantial deficit I suggest that the government should be giving consideration to using the Export Credits Insurance Act in a much wider field than that in which it is at present being used.

In the last two years this act has been of advantage in the selling of some of Canada's primary products. In the sales of substantial quantities of wheat to eastern European countries this act was used as the instrument to provide the necessary credit. The section of the act which allows that to be done is section 2. It is not possible for the Export Credit Insurance Corporation itself to engage in the underwriting of some of these extremely large sales, but the governor in council may authorize the Export Credit Insurance Corporation to underwrite such sales and provide the funds to enable the corporation so to do.
Those sales that were underwritten last year were of substantial advantage to Canada and to prairie grain producers. One of the reasons I am afraid we are in some difficulty in this field is the fact that, as far as eastern European countries are concerned, we have not imported from them goods of anywhere near the value of the goods they have purchased from us.
The figures I have for the first nine months in 1956 show that within that period countries in eastern Europe purchased in Canada goods to the value of $60 million. We purchased from those countries goods to the value of just $6 million. It seems to me it is impossible for us to hope to continue very substantial exports if we are unprepared at the same time to do better than to purchase merely 10 per cent of the value of the goods that have been purchased from us. That is another aspect of the trade picture.
I believe that section 21 of this act should be used right now to provide for the export of a very substantial quantity of wheat to Poland. I hold in my hand the Regina Leader Post of Thursday, February 21, and I see by a Canadian Press dispatch that Poland is engaged at the present time in negotiations for the purchase of a substantial quantity of wheat. Apparently those negotiations are turning on the need of Poland to obtain long-term credit. This report states that Poland is asking for credit for a five-year term. I do not know whether that is the state of the negotiations at the present time, but it seems to me that if that is all that is necessary in order to sell large quantities of wheat to Poland'-and she purchased 13 million bushels from us last year-parliament should have no hesitation in providing through the Export Credits Insurance Act the funds and the guarantee necessary to provide this very important credit so this greatly needed sale might be made.
Therefore I suggest to the parliamentary assistant that he bring to the attention of the minister the opinion of the members of this group, and I would hope of the members of

other groups in this house, that the Export Credits Insurance Act should be expanded at this time in the way I have outlined, and more particularly that credit, in whatever amount may be necessary, should be provided at this time, over whatever period of time may be necessary, in order that Poland may buy a substantial quantity of wheat from us.
The disturbing part of this dispatch, along with a dispatch on the following day in the same paper, written by the Ottawa correspondent, Robert Moon, is that the Polish trade delegates are probably going from Canada to Washington. According to this report, if a wheat deal is not made in Canada then there is a real possibility that a wheat deal may be made between Poland and the United States. I believe that Canada and the members of this house generally would support the government in providing whatever credit may be necessary for whatever period, up to a term of five years as suggested in this report, in order that such an important transaction might be made.
We in this group support the provisions of the bill, Mr. Speaker. We hope the government will use this public instrument as a means of effectively expanding Canada's export trade.

He is quite willing to forget the fact that private industry ever had anything to do with the building of Canada. That is the tone of the C.C.F. all along the line. It has nothing to do with the charge. The rates went up this year in order to enable the companies to carry on the insurance business in a proper manner, which is something you people in Saskatchewan never learned anything about. You are infants in the business. This country could never have reached the place it is today if it had not been for men putting their hands in their pockets 100 years ago and founding the old Halifax Insurance Company, which is over 100 years old. It has stood the test of time and has paid every loss. It has satisfied policyholders. They never needed men like you to run that company. I venture to say there is not a man in your group today who could run an insurance company.
The members of the C.C.F. group are advocates of the government taking over something they know nothing about. If the insuring of the commodities which are being exported was handed over to the legitimate insurance companies-they have the reserves; they do not need to build up reserves since they have them available, made through their actual business experience-we would not need this act. When we hear men like you talk glibly about these things and about the government taking over industry 100 per cent,
I say God help the people if they take over any more.

Export Credits Insurance Act

This government, Mr. Speaker, has put this country in the position in which it finds itself today with our imports and exports out of balance. That is what has caused it. It is not simply because the government have not run the business; it is that they have not run the government.

The hon. member for Eglinton raised the question of the principle of the bill. The principle of the bill of course is simply to improve the ability of the Export Credits Insurance Corporation to serve Canadian exporters and to make Canadian exports more competitive in foreign markets, where they are finding that the exporters of certain other countries are achieving some advantage by reason of the wider coverage that is available to them through the various types of insurance arrangements provided for the exporters of those countries by their government corporations.
The hon. member also raised the question of the principle of the amendment to the Income Tax Act in 1952 providing for the payment of income tax by proprietary corporations, and how we can justify the proposal in this bill to provide for exemption from income tax for this corporation with respect to their payments into the underwriting reserve-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production

Yes. I just wanted to say that I agree with the hon. member that this

could be expedited by dealing with the questions as they arise in committee.
Concerning the matter of principle, I would point out to the hon. member that the statement of the then minister of finance at the time this policy was introduced related specifically to corporations carrying on business operations which were similar to and in competition with private business. As we go along we may be able to satisfy the hon. member that in this case there is no element of competition with any firm in private business, because these particular risks are not covered by any private insurance organization either in this country or in any country, to the best of my knowledge. That point was raised by the hon. member for Assiniboia as well.
The hon. member for Assiniboia also raised two questions relating to trade with eastern European countries. He laid some stress on the lack of purchases by Canada from those countries. That of course is not strictly relevant to this particular legislation, but since he mentioned it I think in fairness I should point out to him that the Canadian market is an open market. It is open to any exporter in any country to come to Canada and do business and sell his products. There is no restriction imposed by the Canadian government on imports from any part of the world, and it is up to those countries to bring their products here and sell them. I may say that the facilities of the Canadian government have been made available to these countries to assist them wherever that has been required.

The hon. member also raised the question of section 21 of this act, and indicated that he felt it should be used to facilitate the export of wheat. least has been as a result of these activities. The hon. member mentioned the current negotiations with representatives of the government of Poland. speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext: The corporation will insure exports to any country in the world so long as it is satisfied with respect to the credit terms and other circumstances of the transaction.

subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext:
Did the parliamentary
assistant intend to say what I understood him to say, that the corporation would insure in connection with any country in the world?
I think he said that in the case of the United States it did not insure. There is another question I want to ask, and perhaps the parliamentary assistant can answer it as well. How are the rates fixed? Is an attempt made to measure the risk and fix the levy accordingly, or are these rates to some extent arbitrary? Is there, in other words, an effort to "make the punishment fit the crime"?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext: The rates are fixed by the corporation using its best judgment in each individual case depending upon the commodity involved, the country to which the export is being made and the credit terms, that is, the length of credit which is requested by the importer from the exporter.

subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext: Is there any schedule in existence in the nature of a tariff which is open to inspection and which would apply universally to all risks?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext: No, there is no published schedule of rates or anything of that kind.

subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext: What assurance is there of any uniformity in the calculation of premiums? How is one to understand that there is no discrimination in the writing of risks?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the assurance with respect to that is that the corporation attempts to do the maximum amount of business it can, and to provide the maximum amount of protection for Canadian exporters consistent with reasonable standards of safety, good business and insurance practice.

subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext:
That is very interesting as a general statement, but I think the committee needs to know how this works out in practice. Do two or three men sit down to establish the rate with regard to each application? What assurance has the house that there is any uniformity in the treatment of applicants in comparable circumstances? How are we

to know that applicant A is charged the same rate on the same type of risk as applicant B?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am informed that in this field policies are issued to individual exporters on a blanket basis for a period of one year; that the risks are assumed under that policy in accordance with applications by exporters in respect of individual exports to various countries, and that the rate is fixed in connection with each of these applications in accordance with the considerations which I have explained, namely the commodity involved, the country to which it is destined and the credit terms proposed between the importer in the foreign country and the exporter. The rate is thus fixed with the idea of attempting to provide coverage for that particular export in a way which will assist the exporter in securing the business for his company.
These are decisions which, naturally, have to be made in the ordinary course of an insurance business of this kind. These matters are not only considered by the operating head of the corporation and his officials, but are reviewed by the board of directors and the advisory board.

subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext: Do members of the board and the advisory board review the rate that is established with regard to every risk?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext: Yes, they are reviewed at each directors' meeting, Mr. Chairman. I am advised that there is a tariff schedule which is not published but which is approved by the board of directors as a general tariff schedule for the guidance of the staff of the corporation and that the rate to be applied with regard to a particular application is considered in relation to that norm.

subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext: I wonder if the parliamentary assistant could say whether every application is accepted or whether some applications are considered too risky and are rejected altogether; and, if so, what proportion of the applications for insurance have been turned down?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am afraid we have no exact statistics regarding the number of risks turned down. Hundreds of applications are received every month, but I am informed that there are few which cannot be arranged in some way or other by the corporation so there would be some sort of insurance coverage given to the exporter.
It might be of interest to the committee to learn that of the blanket policies issued by the corporation since its inception, only 212 have not been renewed. Of this number, 184 were not renewed because the exporter
Export Credits Insurance Act went out of the export business, and 11 were not renewed because the exporter wished to select certain risks for coverage and exclude others. Seven only were not renewed because the corporation refused to renew them.

subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext: May I ask the parliamentary assistant whether the majority of these policies are placed with the corporation by export agencies on behalf of manufacturers, or do they purchase the goods directly and export them themselves, or does the manufacturer place the policy?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext: Approximately 75 per cent of the policies are issued to the manufacturers of the goods to be exported; the balance to others.

subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext: Export agencies?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext: I am still puzzled about the fact that insurance is not written on exports to the United States although it is written on exports to the United Kingdom. The reason given for insurance not being written on exports to the United States is that there are commercial companies doing that type of business. Would that not also be true with regard to Britain? Surely there must be companies writing such insurance in the case of the United Kingdom. For instance, would Lloyd's not write that type of insurance?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext: I am advised that this is one type of business that is not written by any commercial company or any private company, and if there is to be any insurance it has to be written by this corporation. The only reason we write it is that exporters apply for coverage on these exports.

subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext: Have the private companies ever been asked whether they would write this insurance for you?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext: I am advised that it is known that many private companies have looked into the possibility of covering risks of this kind, but they have all decided not to enter the field because of the risks involved and the impossibility of dealing with the matter from a strictly actuarial point of view.

subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext:
The parliamentary assistant said there were three things taken into consideration in arriving at the rate; first, the commodity; second, the country concerned; and third, the nature of the credit arrangement made. Taking the question of the country concerned, one of the things that arises is the very hazard which has arisen in the case of Turkey, the matter of exchange. How is that assessed in fixing the rate? Does the exporter have to assume what is assessed
1722	HOUSE OF
Export Credits Insurance Act as the proper rate to take care of a possible advance in exchange or depreciation of exchange?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext: I am advised that the corporation does not insure against depreciation of exchange. It insures against non-payment of the amount owing by reason of exchange difficulties, and it calculates the premium on the basis of its assessment of the possibilities of non-payment coming about by reason of exchange difficulties during the length of time the particular transaction is to be covered. That is a matter of judgment based on all the information the corporation can secure with respect to balance of payments and the state of the currency of the particular country.

subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext: Are all sales made payable in dollars?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext:
Canadian dollars, United
States dollars or sterling.

subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext:
Before we leave clause 1, I have a question or two. I drew attention to the fact that between December 31, 1955, and September 30,	1956, the corporation
evidently found it necessary to dip into the underwriting reserve to the extent of more than $1,300,000. Has the parliamentary assistant the figures up to December 31, 1956, and will he explain shortly why there was this substantial diminution in the reserve in 1956?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext: The figure for the underwriting reserve at December 31, 1955, was $2,819,326. Between that date and September 30, 1956 claims paid amounted to $1,479,133. The corporation also paid income tax of $282,631, leaving a balance in the underwriting reserve of $1,507,119.

subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext: What was the position at December 31? Are those figures available?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext: I am advised that they are just being prepared. The final figure for December 31, 1956 is not yet available but it should be available within the next few days.

subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext: What specifically caused the substantial losses in 1956? Were they all the result of Turkey's shortage of foreign exchange?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext: It was principally blocked exchange in Turkey and Colombia.

subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext:
Are you aware of the fact that all insurance companies in Canada must file their annual statements for the period up to the end of December by tomorrow? Yet this great, efficient corporation of the government is not going to have its statement in until three or four days later.


I wish every private corporation had that much leeway. That shows the efficiency of the government. This very government demands these figures from other insurance companies operating in Canada by the 28th day of February; yet they come in here and glibly say to the House of Commons that they will be ready three or four days later.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext: As a matter of . fact the requirement applying to this corporation is March 31, 1957.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 2-Deduction, for income tax, of credits to underwriting reserve.

subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext:
I indicated when speaking on second reading that we would require on the part of the government ample justification for the proposed departure from the principle laid down by the government itself in 1952. This is the clause under which the corporation is now to be exempted from income tax until the underwriting reserve has been built up to a total of $5 million. I remind the house again that the principle was clearly laid down by the then minister of finance in 1952 that crown corporations designated as proprietary corporations, and up to that time exempt from income tax, should in future pay corporation income tax to the federal government in the same manner as any privately owned corporation.
All that the parliamentary assistant has been able to say to us by way of justification is that this corporation is engaged in insurance in a field where it is not competing directly with privately owned corporations. But, sir, that is not a sound basis of distinction. The government itself initiated the statutory designation of the Export Credits Insurance Corporation as one of the proprietary corporations under schedule D of the Financial Administration Act. That showed quite clearly their estimation of what should be the application of the principle laid down by Mr. Abbott in 1952 with respect to this particular corporation. If there is any justification for this departure from a sound principle recognized and accepted by the house then and ever since, we are interested in hearing it, but we have not heard any justification yet for this proposed departure.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext:
I can assure the committee that there is sound justification for this amendment, and that there is no attempt to derogate in any way from the principle laid down in 1952, which the hon. member was good enough to describe as a sound principle. The fact is that all private insurance companies are entitled under the Income Tax Act to set up reserves free of income tax. The purpose and effect of this clause is

simply to extend the same privilege to this company which, under the wording of the Income Tax Act, is not entitled to the privilege which is extended to other insurance companies. It is simply to place this company under the same requirements with respect to income tax and the setting up of reserves as those which apply to insurance companies generally under the legislation that is applicable to them.

subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext: That is an interesting statement. I point out that it is diametrically opposed to what the parliamentary assistant himself said just a few minutes ago on this very same subject. If there is ample opportunity afforded to private insurance corporations to set up comparable reserves and to enjoy exemption from income tax in respect of them, then I fail to see the necessity for special legislation such as is proposed in this particular clause. It is evident that the Export Credits Insurance Corporation, as a crown proprietary corporation, is entitled to all the benefits of the Income Tax Act, as is any private insurance company. We shall now need some explanation to reconcile two statements by the parliamentary assistant that are directly contradictory of each other.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I do not think there is any requirement for reconciliation. I think the hon. member and I both agreed that this was a matter that could best be fully discussed at the committee stage. But in my opening remarks I referred to the particular wording which the hon. member himself had quoted from the statement by the minister of finance in 1952, and I simply contented myself with pointing out to him the distinction which applies in this case but which is not the full explanation which has now been given to him. I assure the hon. member that the state of the law now is that the provisions of the Income Tax Act which permit private insurance companies to set up their reserves free of income tax-

subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext: Has the parliamentary assistant the reference? Can he give us the clause which is referred to?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext:
I have not the act with me. I think it is section 87, but I am not sure. In any event, the Department of National Revenue have ruled that this exemption does not apply to this particular company, while it does apply to private companies. The purpose of this amendment is simply to put this corporation on an equal footing with other insurance companies, and to give them similar treatment with respect to income tax.
Export Credits Insurance Act

subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext: Does the parliamentary assistant mean that the usual reserve for unexpired premiums that is allowed in a private company would not be allowed in this particular corporation?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman. This is not a premium reserve. It is an underwriting reserve to cover possible losses and has nothing to do with a reserve such as that mentioned by my hon. friend. I presume you mean the reserve for unearned premiums?

subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext: No, this is not that type of reserve at all. It is simply the underwriting reserve which was originally established by the corporation as a reserve account and which in 1954 was set up by the amending bill that session as a statutory underwriting reserve with a maximum of $5 million.

subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext: Is it not true that the Department of National Revenue will allow this company to write off losses if, as and when they actually occur?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext: Yes, that is correct. Losses of about $176,000, approximately, have been written off in that way.

subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext: Is it not also true that the Department of National Revenue, if you can show a risk account receivable-that you have a risk that you are going to face-will allow the corporation to set that up as a reserve, deductible for tax purposes the same as any account receivable in ordinary business if it is proved bad?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext: I am advised that this corporation is not in a position to take advantage of that kind of an arrangement because of the long period of time over which a risk is carried and the fact that the loss may occur, for example, at the end of a five-year period of the policy. There is no way in which they can judge in the first year of the policy whether or not any reserve should be set up for that particular possibility of loss.

subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in the
December 31, 1954, statement I notice at the back the analysis by countries of the actual risks underwritten during 1954. I notice $5,800,000, approximately, to Turkey. Is it part of that amount that it is now being proposed to take care of?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext: Yes. At least part of these risks is included in the payments that have been made this year under the loss payments.

subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext:
You paid out $1,479,000, not necessarily all of it applying to Turkey. But has the balance from Turkey been collected?

Export Credits Insurance Act

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext: No. So far there has been no recovery under the loss payments in respect of Turkish risks.

subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext: Before we call it six o'clock, Mr. Chairman, I should like to get one point clear. I understood the parliamentary assistant to say that the corporation was now in a worse position than is a private insurance company. As I read section 2, it seems to me that it will put the corporation in a better position than a private company, in that it may credit to the underwriting reserve any amount it wishes to credit to that reserve and that amount will all be tax deductible. Certainly that is a privilege no private insurance corporation would have. In other words, the discretion as to how much will be tax deductible is left entirely with the corporation. I should like to know whether the amendment does not put the corporation in a better position than the private company.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext:
Section 11 (a) of the act of incorporation requires the corporation to credit to the underwriting reserve the entire excess of its revenues over its disbursements in a fiscal year. Hence the corporation has no discretion at all. It is required by statute to credit the entire excess to the underwriting reserve until the underwriting reserve reaches the maximum set out in the statute which is $5 million. There is no possibility of the corporation exercising any discretion

with respect to that matter. It all has to go into the underwriting reserve.

subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext: Perhaps before resumption of discussion of this matter the parliamentary assistant would consider what the answer would be to the question whether that does not put this corporation in a better position, taxwise, than the private corporation.
